answer.observations: Default run r001: UDP delivers its offered 300 Mbps with zero loss, TCP delivers 299,885,434 bps, and link_util is only 0.618. Thus about 382 Mbps of link capacity is idle, while TCP's configured scheduler share at weightUdp=0.5 is 500 Mbps. The central unexplained fact is why TCP does not use either its configured share or the idle link capacity. TCP's measured payload rate is also almost exactly equal to UDP's, which may be a scheduler artifact or a coincidence. I need cwnd, queue occupancy, and queue-minimum traces for r001 to distinguish a TCP congestion-window/buffer limit from a scheduler service limit.

whys.result: TCP goodput is about 300 Mbps even though its configured scheduler share is 500 Mbps and the link is only 61.8% utilized.
whys.guess: TCP's own congestion control or socket buffer keeps its congestion window too small, so throughput is cwnd/RTT limited rather than scheduler limited.
whys.unseen: The cwnd trajectory, actual RTT, and whether q_band1 or q_band0 is persistently nonempty in r001.
whys.matters: If true, changing tcpVariant, queuePkts, or duration may raise TCP goodput, while merely changing weightUdp will not.
whys.reason: A weightUdp reduction that gives TCP more scheduler share should leave TCP unchanged if TCP is self-limited, and should raise TCP if scheduler share is the limit.

whys.guess: The scheduler may allocate service in packet slots or otherwise tie TCP service to UDP traffic, so UDP's unused configured bandwidth is not fully given to TCP.
whys.unseen: The scheduler's service discipline when the UDP queue is underfilled, and the packet-rate share needed to carry UDP without loss.
whys.matters: If true, weightUdp controls both UDP loss and TCP's usable share, and the optimal weight may be just above UDP's packet-rate share.
whys.reason: The proposed weightUdp test directly checks whether giving TCP a larger scheduler share changes TCP goodput.

answer.observations: E0/E1 show default tcp_goodput_bps=299885434 with udp_loss_frac=0, no drops, and link_util=0.618. Lowering weightUdp to 0.35 or 0.40 did not raise TCP by more than tolerance, so at the default 10s measurement TCP is not scheduler-share limited. The r001 series explains part of this: q_band0 and q_band1 are zero, drops are zero, cwnd grows steadily from 105704 to 919480 bytes by t=11.9, and instantaneous tcp_bps rises from 15.7 Mbps to 366.5 Mbps. Thus the measured 300 Mbps average is a ramp average, not a steady-state value. The important unexplained items are: (1) how much higher the 30s average becomes once the ramp is amortized; (2) whether another TCP variant reaches the apparent 1 MB/RTT ceiling much faster than Cubic; and (3) whether weightUdp can be reduced below 0.5 without violating udp_loss_frac <= 0.01.

answer.observations: Default run r001 (E0) has UDP 300.0032 Mbps, TCP 299.8854 Mbps, zero measured drops, and link_util 0.618. The r001 series shows TCP cwnd still increasing through t=12s, so the 10s measured window includes a ramp. X1 (E1/C1) shows weightUdp 0.35 and 0.40 did not raise TCP by more than tolerance at duration 10, supporting that TCP was not scheduler-share limited at that point. X2 (E2) shows duration 30 raises Cubic to 376.5235 Mbps (C2 held), NewReno is lower than Cubic (C3 failed as the rival predicted), and BBR reaches 418.8766 Mbps (C4 held). BBR's 418.876597 Mbps is within 0.13% of 1 MiB / 20 ms = 419.4304 Mbps, which strongly suggests a socket-buffer/minimum-RTT cap. The main unexplained points are: whether BBR's cwnd/queue behavior confirms that cap; whether BBR needs duration 30 or already reaches the cap by duration 10; whether lowering weightUdp to 0.35 changes TCP or UDP loss under BBR; and whether a very small queuePkts=4 causes drops.

answer.observations: The ledger now covers all four knobs. BBR at duration 10 and 30, weightUdp 0.5 and 0.35, and queuePkts 100 and 4 all give tcp_goodput_bps about 418.9 Mbps with udp_loss_frac 0, drops 0, and retransmissions 0 (E3). The remaining TCP variants at duration 30 are below or within tolerance of BBR: TcpLinuxReno 382.4 Mbps, TcpVegas 336.1 Mbps, TcpBic 418.7 Mbps, all with udp_loss_frac 0 (E4, C9). The grep_trace request for cwnd/buffer lines returned no match, but the numeric agreement with 1 MiB / 20 ms and the absence of drops/retransmissions make the buffer/RTT cap the best explanation. No material unexplained result remains; the only unresolved detail is whether TcpBic at duration 10 is exactly indistinguishable from TcpBbr, but the tested duration-30 values are already within tolerance.

report.limit: The result is limited by the fixed 1 MB TCP send/receive buffers and the 20 ms minimum round-trip time: in-flight TCP data cannot exceed about 1 MiB, so payload throughput cannot exceed about 1 MiB / 20 ms = 419.43 Mbps. BBR reaches 418.9 Mbps with zero drops and zero retransmissions, and changing scheduler share, queue size, or measurement duration does not move it. Evidence: C5, C6, C7, C8, E3, E4.
report.explanation: TcpBbr is best because it reaches the buffer/RTT in-flight cap within tolerance, while the other tested variants are below that cap or, in the case of TcpBic, statistically indistinguishable from BBR (C9, E4). At BBR, the scheduler share is not limiting: default weightUdp=0.5 gives TCP 500 Mbps of configured share, above the 419 Mbps cap, and lowering weightUdp to 0.35 gives no TCP gain while UDP loss remains 0 (C7, E3). Queue size is not limiting: queuePkts=4 gives the same TCP goodput and UDP loss as queuePkts=100 (C8, E3). Duration is not limiting for BBR: duration 30 is not more than 1% above duration 10 (C6, E3), although duration did matter for TcpCubic (C2), so the simpler default duration 10 is kept for BBR. The link is not saturated (link_util about 0.746), and there are no drops or retransmissions, so the remaining ceiling is the fixed socket-buffer/RTT product, not the scheduler or queues.
report.holds_when: The fixed 1 MB TCP buffers, 20 ms one-way delay/20 ms minimum RTT, 1 Gbps link, 1500-byte MTU, and 300 Mbps UDP load remain unchanged; the scheduler gives TCP at least about 419 Mbps of usable share; and the UDP loss condition does not force a different weightUdp.
report.breaks_when: If TCP buffers were larger or RTT smaller, the in-flight cap would rise and other settings could become limiting. If weightUdp were raised enough that TCP's configured scheduler share fell below about 419 Mbps, scheduler share would limit TCP. If UDP demand or the loss condition required a different scheduler share, weightUdp would need retuning. If duration were shortened below the tested 10 s so that TCP had not reached steady state, duration could matter.

claims.text: TcpBbr at weightUdp=0.5, queuePkts=100, duration=10 gives tcp_goodput_bps=418901197 with udp_loss_frac=0.
BBR's throughput is at the 1 MiB / 20 ms buffer/RTT cap, not at a scheduler, queue, or link-saturation limit.
No other tested TCP variant validly exceeds BBR by more than 1%; TcpBic is within tolerance, while TcpLinuxReno and TcpVegas are lower.
Lowering weightUdp from 0.5 to 0.35 does not raise TCP goodput and keeps UDP loss at 0.
Reducing queuePkts from 100 to 4 does not change TCP goodput or UDP loss.
For BBR, duration 30 is not meaningfully better than duration 10, although duration mattered for TcpCubic.
At the recommended setting the link is not saturated and there are no drops or TCP retransmissions.
